routines.name: 6ths & 7ths
routines.connectionDescription: The intervals of a 6th and 7th define the extended sound of chords. Drilling these intervals physically while learning to use 7th chords harmonically connects your ear, hands, and brain.

exercises.name: Major 6th Interval Patterns
exercises.description: Play major 6ths (9 frets) on single strings, then across string pairs. Warm, consonant interval.

exercises.name: Minor 7th Interval Patterns
exercises.description: Play minor 7ths (10 frets) — the dominant chord interval. Bluesy, relaxed tension.

exercises.name: Major 7th Interval Patterns
exercises.description: Play major 7ths (11 frets) — one half step below the octave. Beautiful, jazzy dissonance.

exercises.name: Interval Melodies
exercises.description: Create short melodies using only 6th and 7th intervals. Jump between wide intervals for a modern, angular sound.

theoryLessons.title: Replacing Triads with 7th Chords
theoryLessons.content: Any diatonic triad can be enriched by adding its 7th. C→Cmaj7, Dm→Dm7, G→G7. The progression sounds more sophisticated without changing the harmony.

keyPoints.definition: C - Am - F - G (basic triads)
Cmaj7 - Am7 - Fmaj7 - G7 (same progression, richer sound)
Replace I and IV with maj7, ii/iii/vi with m7, V with dom7.

theoryLessons.title: The ii7-V7-Imaj7 Foundation
theoryLessons.content: The most important progression in jazz. Dm7→G7→Cmaj7 in C major. The guide tones of each chord resolve by half step to the next, creating irresistible forward motion.

keyPoints.definition: Dm7 (F,C) → G7 (F,B) → Cmaj7 (E,B). The F stays, C drops to B, then F drops to E. Smooth.
Learn ii-V-I in C, G, D, A, F, Bb at minimum.
Add vi7 at the end: Dm7-G7-Cmaj7-Am7 → loops back to Dm7.

theoryLessons.title: Tritone Substitution Preview
theoryLessons.content: The tritone (b5 interval) inside every V7 chord can be exploited: the V7 can be replaced by a dom7 chord a tritone away. G7 → Db7. Both share the same guide tones (B/F = Cb/F). Mind-bending but powerful.

keyPoints.definition: Db7. Both contain B(Cb) and F.
Dm7 → Db7 → Cmaj7 (bass walks down: D-Db-C)
You'll master this in the Advanced course. For now, just know it exists.

routines.name: Articulation & Swing
routines.connectionDescription: Articulation is HOW you say something; modes are WHAT you say. Each mode has a unique color/mood, and your articulation choices either reinforce or transform that mood.

exercises.name: Staccato vs Legato Control
exercises.description: Play the same G major scale phrase twice: first with short, detached staccato notes (mute between each), then with smooth, connected legato. Same notes, completely different feel.

exercises.name: Swing Feel — Triplet Shuffle
exercises.description: Play eighth notes with a swing feel: long-short, long-short (triplet-based). This is the groove of blues, jazz, and classic rock. Practice with a shuffle backing track.

exercises.name: Hybrid Picking Introduction
exercises.description: Use your pick for lower strings and fingers (m, a) for higher strings simultaneously. This lets you play bass notes and melody at the same time.

exercises.name: Dynamic Control — Soft to Loud
exercises.description: Play the same phrase at pianissimo (very soft), mezzo-forte (medium), and fortissimo (very loud). Control your pick attack to change volume without changing tone.

theoryLessons.title: The 7 Modes of the Major Scale
theoryLessons.content: Each degree of the major scale can serve as a starting point for a mode. Starting C major from C = Ionian. From D = Dorian. From E = Phrygian. Same notes, different root, completely different sound.

keyPoints.definition: The major scale itself. Bright, happy. I chord.
Minor with a bright 6th. Funky, soulful. ii chord.
Minor with a dark b2. Spanish, exotic. iii chord.
Major with a raised 4th. Dreamy, floating. IV chord.
Major with a b7. Bluesy, dominant. V chord.
Natural minor scale. Dark, sad. vi chord.
Diminished sound. Unstable, tense. vii° chord.

theoryLessons.title: Characteristic Notes
theoryLessons.content: Each mode has one or two notes that make it unique compared to plain major or minor. These 'characteristic notes' are what you emphasize to bring out the mode's flavor.

keyPoints.definition: Natural 6th (major 6th in a minor context). This is what separates it from Aeolian.
b2 (half step above root). Instantly 'Spanish' sounding.
Raised 4th (#4). Dreamy, 'floating' quality.
b7 (minor 7th in a major context). Bluesy, dominant.

theoryLessons.title: Modes Are Not Just Scales
theoryLessons.content: A common mistake: thinking modes are just scales you play over any chord. A mode only sounds like itself when played over its matching chord. D Dorian sounds Dorian over a Dm or Dm7 vamp — NOT over a C major chord (that's just C Ionian starting from D).

keyPoints.definition: The chord defines the mode, not the notes. Same notes over different chords = different modes.
Play D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D over a Dm7 chord. NOW it sounds Dorian.
A mode needs its root chord to anchor the sound. No chord context = no modal sound.

routines.name: Dorian Mode
routines.connectionDescription: Dorian is the most practical mode for intermediate players — it's everywhere in blues, rock, funk, and jazz. The theory teaches you how to select and apply any mode, while the practice gives you hands-on fluency.

exercises.name: D Dorian Scale — E Shape
exercises.description: Play D Dorian (D-E-F-G-A-B-C-D) in the E-shape position at fret 10. Same notes as C major but rooted on D. Over a Dm7 vamp, this sounds completely different from C major.

exercises.name: Dorian vs Aeolian Comparison
exercises.description: Play D Dorian then D Aeolian (natural minor) back to back over Dm7. The ONLY difference is the 6th: Dorian has B natural, Aeolian has Bb. Hear how the natural 6th makes Dorian brighter.

exercises.name: Dorian Licks
exercises.description: Three signature Dorian licks that highlight the natural 6th. These licks only sound 'Dorian' because they emphasize B (the characteristic note) over Dm.

exercises.name: Dorian Improvisation Over Dm7 Vamp
exercises.description: Set up a Dm7 loop (or use a backing track) and improvise using only D Dorian. Target the characteristic 6th (B) to bring out the modal flavor.

theoryLessons.title: Applying Modes to Progressions
theoryLessons.content: Modes work best over static chords or simple vamps. Over a Dm7 groove, play D Dorian. Over a G7 groove, play G Mixolydian. The chord tells you which mode to use.

keyPoints.definition: Dm7 → D Dorian. G7 → G Mixolydian. Cmaj7 → C Ionian (or Lydian for color).
Dm7-G7 alternating: D Dorian over Dm7, G Mixolydian over G7. Or just use C major over both (they're in the same key).
Over a ii-V-I in C (Dm7-G7-Cmaj7): you CAN play each mode, or just use C major throughout. Your choice depends on how much modal color you want.

theoryLessons.title: Modal Interchange
theoryLessons.content: Borrowing chords or scales from parallel modes. In C major, you can borrow the bVII chord (Bb) from C Mixolydian, or the iv chord (Fm) from C minor. This adds unexpected color to otherwise predictable progressions.

keyPoints.definition: In C major: use Bb chord. Classic rock sound (C-Bb-F).
In C major: use Fm instead of F. Dark, dramatic.
In C major: use Eb chord. Creates a powerful shift.

theoryLessons.title: Creating Modal Compositions
theoryLessons.content: To compose in a mode: establish the root chord firmly, emphasize the characteristic note in your melody, and avoid notes/chords that would pull you back to the parent major key.

keyPoints.definition: Vamp on Dm7. Melody uses B natural prominently. Avoid resolving to C major.
Vamp on G7 or G. Melody emphasizes F natural. Avoid resolving to C major.
Vamp on Cmaj7#11. Melody emphasizes F#. Ethereal, floating quality.

routines.name: Major Scale — Full Neck
routines.connectionDescription: This is where everything clicks. The CAGED system is the map that connects every scale shape, chord shape, and arpeggio on the entire fretboard. Filling in the scale blanks while understanding CAGED organization means you can finally see the whole neck as one unified system.

exercises.name: G and D Shape Major Scales
exercises.description: Learn the final two CAGED positions: G-shape (position 4) and D-shape (position 5). In the key of G major, these fill in the remaining gaps between your E, C, and A shapes. Now you have all 5 positions.

exercises.name: All 5 Positions Connected — Ascending
exercises.description: Play G major ascending through all 5 CAGED positions from the lowest fret to the highest: E-shape → D-shape → C-shape → A-shape → G-shape. Cover the entire neck in one key without stopping.

exercises.name: Horizontal Scale Runs
exercises.description: Instead of playing vertically within a position, play along a single string from open to fret 12. Then on two strings. Then three. This trains horizontal fretboard vision — seeing scales as lines, not boxes.

exercises.name: Circle of 4ths Scale Practice
exercises.description: Play the major scale in every key following the Circle of 4ths: C-F-Bb-Eb-Ab-Db-Gb-B-E-A-D-G. Play each scale in the E-shape position. This forces you to know every key's notes instantly.

theoryLessons.title: CAGED as a Fretboard Organization System
theoryLessons.content: CAGED isn't just 5 scale shapes — it's a complete system that connects chords, scales, and arpeggios across the entire neck. Each CAGED shape has a matching chord shape, scale pattern, arpeggio pattern, and pentatonic pattern. They're all the same map viewed through different lenses.

keyPoints.definition: C chord shape → C-shape scale → C-shape arpeggio. All occupy the same fret zone.
A chord shape → A-shape scale → A-shape arpeggio. Same zone, different note selections.
G chord shape (the awkward one) → G-shape scale → G-shape arpeggio.
E chord shape (most common barre) → E-shape scale → E-shape arpeggio.
D chord shape → D-shape scale → D-shape arpeggio.

theoryLessons.title: Connecting Chords, Scales, and Arpeggios
theoryLessons.content: In any key, the chord shape tells you where the scale lives, and the arpeggio is the chord tones extracted from the scale. If you can see the barre chord, you can see the scale; if you can see the scale, you can see the arpeggios.

keyPoints.definition: See the G barre chord (E-shape, fret 3). The E-shape scale pattern surrounds it.
Inside the E-shape scale, the R-3-5 notes = the barre chord. Pull them out = arpeggio.
In any position, you can instantly switch between chords, scales, and arpeggios without moving your hand.

theoryLessons.title: Finding Any Chord Tone Anywhere
theoryLessons.content: With all 5 CAGED positions memorized, you can find any note of any chord anywhere on the neck. Need the 3rd of Bb? Find Bb on a string, count up 4 half steps = D. Or use the CAGED pattern to locate the 3rd within the nearest position.

keyPoints.definition: Know all root notes across 6 strings. Octave patterns connect them.
In each CAGED shape, the 3rd is always in the same relative position to the root.
Similarly, the 5th has a consistent position within each shape.
One fret below the root (for major 7th) or two frets below (for minor 7th).

routines.name: Four Triad Types
routines.connectionDescription: Triads are the building blocks of extended chords. A Dom13 chord contains a major triad, a minor triad built on the 5th, and more. Understanding all four triad types means you can deconstruct any extended chord into manageable shapes.

exercises.name: Major, Minor, Diminished, Augmented — Comparison
exercises.description: Play all four triad types from the same root (C) on string set 1-2-3: C major (C-E-G), C minor (C-Eb-G), C diminished (C-Eb-Gb), C augmented (C-E-G#). Hear how each quality sounds.

exercises.name: All Inversions — All Types
exercises.description: Play each of the four triad types in root position, 1st inversion, and 2nd inversion. That's 12 shapes on one string set. Then repeat on string sets 2-3-4 and 3-4-5.

exercises.name: Triad Pairs — Upper Structures
exercises.description: Play two triads back to back that together outline a 7th chord. Example: C major + Dm = Cmaj9 sound. E major + G major over C = C major extension sound. This is upper structure triad voicing.

exercises.name: Triad Arpeggios Across the Neck
exercises.description: Play C major triad arpeggios connecting all CAGED positions. Start in position 1, arpeggiate R-3-5, shift to next position, continue. Cover the whole neck.

theoryLessons.title: The Four Triad Types
theoryLessons.content: There are only four possible triads built from stacking major and minor 3rds. Major (M3+m3), Minor (m3+M3), Diminished (m3+m3), Augmented (M3+M3). Every chord in music is built from these four foundations.

keyPoints.definition: Major 3rd + minor 3rd. Bright, stable. C-E-G.
Minor 3rd + major 3rd. Dark, melancholic. C-Eb-G.
Minor 3rd + minor 3rd. Tense, unstable. C-Eb-Gb.
Major 3rd + major 3rd. Mysterious, unresolved. C-E-G#.

theoryLessons.title: 9th Chord Voicings
theoryLessons.content: 9th chords add color to 7th chords. Cmaj9 = C-E-G-B-D. On guitar, we often drop the 5th: C-E-B-D. The 9th (D) adds a shimmering quality. Three types: maj9, min9, dom9.

keyPoints.definition: Cmaj9 = C-E-G-B-D. Dreamy, lush. I chord in jazz.
Cm9 = C-Eb-G-Bb-D. Cool, sophisticated. ii chord sound.
C9 = C-E-G-Bb-D. Funky, bluesy. V chord with extra color.

theoryLessons.title: 11th and 13th Chords
theoryLessons.content: Keep stacking 3rds: 9th + 11th = 11th chord. 11th + 13th = 13th chord. A 13th chord contains all 7 notes of the scale. On guitar, we voice these selectively — R, 3, 7, plus the extension.

keyPoints.definition: Add the 11th (= 4th). Caution: the 11th clashes with the major 3rd. Often used as sus or #11.
Add the 13th (= 6th). C13 = R-3-b7-13 on guitar. Classic soul/funk voicing.
Cmaj7#11 = C-E-G-B-F#. The #11 avoids the clash and creates a Lydian flavor.
Keep R-3-7 and add the extension. Drop the 5th (it's boring). 4-note voicings are plenty.

routines.name: Advanced 16th Rhythms
routines.connectionDescription: Advanced rhythmic control combined with modal mastery gives you complete musical independence. You can play any rhythmic figure over any modal context — the ultimate combination for improvisation and composition.

exercises.name: Dotted Rhythms
exercises.description: Play dotted eighth + sixteenth note patterns. The dot adds half the note's value, creating a long-short feel different from swing. This is the rhythm of marches, Celtic music, and many pop songs.

exercises.name: Tied Notes and Syncopation
exercises.description: Play 16th note patterns where notes tie across beat boundaries. The attack happens on an upbeat and sustains through the downbeat. This creates extreme syncopation — the heartbeat of funk and Latin music.

exercises.name: Rhythmic Displacement
exercises.description: Take a simple 4-note pattern and start it on different 16th-note subdivisions: beat 1, the 'e', the '&', the 'a'. Same notes, four completely different grooves.

exercises.name: Polyrhythmic Awareness — 3 Against 4
exercises.description: While tapping quarter notes with your foot (4), play triplets with your hands (3). Then reverse. This trains rhythmic independence — essential for advanced soloing.

theoryLessons.title: Mode-Chord Matching in Real Songs
theoryLessons.content: Modes aren't just theory exercises — they're the sound of real music. Dorian = 'So What' by Miles Davis. Mixolydian = 'Sweet Home Alabama' riff. Phrygian = flamenco. Lydian = 'Flying in a Blue Dream' by Joe Satriani.

keyPoints.definition: So What, Oye Como Va, Evil Ways, Moondance
Sweet Home Alabama (riff), Norwegian Wood, Sweet Child O Mine (verse)
White Rabbit (verse), War (Low Rider)
Flying in a Blue Dream, The Simpsons theme, Dreams by Fleetwood Mac (intro)

theoryLessons.title: Mixing Modes Within a Progression
theoryLessons.content: Over a changing progression, you can switch modes with each chord. Over Dm7 play Dorian, over G7 play Mixolydian, over Cmaj7 play Ionian. Or you can play one scale throughout and let the chords create the modal color.

keyPoints.definition: Maximum color change. Each chord gets its own flavor. More complex to execute.
Simpler. Let the chord changes create the modal shifts naturally.
Use one scale mostly, but emphasize characteristic notes as chords change.

theoryLessons.title: Advanced Modal Analysis
theoryLessons.content: Analyze progressions to determine which modes apply. If chords are diatonic to one key, use that key's modes. If chords are from different keys, each chord may need its own scale — this is 'chord-scale theory.'

keyPoints.definition: Dm7-G7-Cmaj7 = all in C major. Use C major modes: D Dorian, G Mixolydian, C Ionian.
Dm7-Db7-Cmaj7 (tritone sub). Db7 is NOT in C major. Use Db Mixolydian or Db Lydian Dominant.
Single chord for many bars = pure modal playing. The chord IS the mode.

routines.name: Triads & Major Scales
routines.connectionDescription: Triad-based soloing IS chord substitution in action. When you solo using a different triad over a chord (e.g., playing Em shapes over C), you're creating the sound of extensions. The theory explains why this works.

exercises.name: Diatonic Triad Sequences — All String Sets
exercises.description: Play all 7 diatonic triads in C major ascending up the neck on each string set. Root position only first, then mix inversions. This maps the entire harmony across the fretboard.

exercises.name: Triad-Based Soloing
exercises.description: Solo over a Cmaj7 chord using Em triad shapes. Em (E-G-B) over C gives you the 3-5-7 of Cmaj7 — instant jazz sound without knowing 'jazz scales.' Then try Am triad over C (gives you 6-1-3 = C6 sound).

exercises.name: Triad Pairs Over ii-V-I
exercises.description: Over Dm7: play Dm+F triads. Over G7: play G+Bdim triads. Over Cmaj7: play C+Em triads. Each pair outlines the 7th chord's extensions.

exercises.name: Connecting Triads into Melodic Lines
exercises.description: Use triad arpeggios as launching points for melodic phrases. Arpeggiate a triad, then connect to the next triad with scale tones. This creates lines that clearly outline the harmony.

theoryLessons.title: Chord Substitution Principles
theoryLessons.content: A chord substitution replaces one chord with another that shares common tones or function. The simplest: replace any chord with one that shares 2+ notes. C (C-E-G) can be replaced by Am (A-C-E) or Em (E-G-B) — they share 2 notes each.

keyPoints.definition: Replace a chord with one from the same key that shares notes. I↔iii, I↔vi, IV↔ii.
Replace a chord with one that has the same harmonic function. Any minor can sub for another minor in the same key.
Shared notes maintain the harmonic color. Differences add variety without clashing.

theoryLessons.title: Tritone Substitution
theoryLessons.content: The most powerful substitution in jazz. Any dominant 7th chord can be replaced by the dom7 a tritone (6 half steps) away. G7 → Db7. Both contain the same tritone interval (B-F = Cb-F), so they resolve the same way.

keyPoints.definition: G7 (G-B-D-F) and Db7 (Db-F-Ab-Cb). Shared guide tones: B/Cb and F.
ii-V-I becomes Dm7-Db7-Cmaj7. Bass walks D-Db-C (chromatic descent). Beautiful.
Any V7 in any key can take a tritone sub. Ab7 for D7, Eb7 for A7, etc.

theoryLessons.title: Diminished Chord Substitution
theoryLessons.content: Diminished 7th chords are symmetrical — they repeat every 3 frets. This means each dim7 chord can function as a dominant substitute for 4 different keys. Bdim7 can resolve to C, Eb, Gb, or A.

keyPoints.definition: C → C#dim7 → Dm7. The dim7 chromatically connects two diatonic chords.
Bdim7 → C = same as G7b9 → C (Bdim7 contains the top 4 notes of G7b9).
Bdim7 = Ddim7 = Fdim7 = Abdim7. All the same chord, different names.

routines.name: Triads to 7th Chords
routines.connectionDescription: Diminished and augmented chords break the symmetry of major/minor. Understanding these 'exotic' chord types while practicing the connection from triads to 7ths gives you the complete chord vocabulary.

exercises.name: Building 7ths from Triads
exercises.description: Start with a triad shape, then add the 7th. C major triad → add B = Cmaj7. Add Bb = C7. Dm triad → add C = Dm7. Physical construction of 7th chords from shapes you know.

exercises.name: Guide Tone Lines — 3rd and 7th Voice Leading
exercises.description: Play only the 3rd and 7th of each chord through a ii-V-I-vi progression. These two notes voice-lead by half steps, creating smooth connected lines.

exercises.name: 7th Chord Arpeggios — All CAGED Positions
exercises.description: Play Cmaj7 arpeggios (C-E-G-B) in all 5 CAGED positions. Then Dm7, G7, Am7. Four-note arpeggios across the full neck.

exercises.name: Walking Bass + Chord Comping
exercises.description: Play bass notes on beats 1 and 3 (root and 5th) while strumming the chord on beats 2 and 4. Alternating bass pattern — the foundation of fingerstyle jazz and folk.

theoryLessons.title: Diminished Chord Construction
theoryLessons.content: Diminished triads stack two minor 3rds: R-b3-b5. Diminished 7th chords add another minor 3rd: R-b3-b5-bb7 (bb7 = 6th enharmonically). The result is a perfectly symmetrical chord that divides the octave into equal parts.

keyPoints.definition: C-Eb-Gb. Two minor 3rds stacked. Tense, unstable.
C-Eb-Gb-Bbb(A). Three minor 3rds stacked. Maximum symmetry.
C-Eb-Gb-Bb. Less tense than full dim7. The vii chord in major keys.
Cdim7 = Ebdim7 = Gbdim7 = Adim7. Move up 3 frets = same chord.

theoryLessons.title: Augmented Chord Construction
theoryLessons.content: Augmented triads stack two major 3rds: R-3-#5. Like diminished, augmented chords are symmetrical — they divide the octave into three equal parts (every 4 frets).

keyPoints.definition: C-E-G#. Two major 3rds stacked. Mysterious, dreamlike.
Caug = Eaug = G#aug. Move up 4 frets = same chord.
Aug chords typically resolve up by half step: Caug → F (the #5 moves up to the root of the next chord).
Passing chord between I and vi: C → Caug → Am. The G moves to G# moves to A.

theoryLessons.title: Dim and Aug in Progressions
theoryLessons.content: Diminished chords function as leading-tone chords (pull up by half step to the next chord). Augmented chords function as altered dominant chords (the #5 creates tension that resolves). Both add chromatic color.

keyPoints.definition: C → C#dim7 → Dm7. Chromatic bass: C-C#-D.
G7 can become G7b9 → contains Bdim7. Bdim7 → C resolves the same.
G+ → C. The #5 (D#) resolves up to E (3rd of C). Dramatic resolution.
C → C+ → F. Bass stays on C while G rises to G# to A (in F chord).

routines.name: Pentatonic Mastery
routines.connectionDescription: Advanced pentatonic mastery combined with harmonic minor theory expands your tonal palette dramatically. The harmonic minor's raised 7th creates exotic intervals that sound completely different from pentatonic — giving you contrast between familiar and exotic.

exercises.name: All 5 Pentatonic Positions Fluently
exercises.description: Play the A minor pentatonic in all 5 positions, connecting them seamlessly. You should be able to start in any position and flow into any adjacent position without hesitation.

exercises.name: Pentatonic Sequences — Groups of 3, 4, and 6
exercises.description: Play the pentatonic in sequences: groups of 3 (1-2-3, 2-3-4...), groups of 4 (1-2-3-4, 2-3-4-5...), and groups of 6. These break you out of the linear up-down habit.

exercises.name: Connecting Positions Horizontally
exercises.description: Play pentatonic licks that start in one position and slide into the next. Use slides on a single string to shift positions smoothly. Cover positions 1→2→3→4→5 in one continuous phrase.

exercises.name: Advanced Pentatonic Techniques
exercises.description: Combine bends, slides, hammer-ons, pull-offs, and double-stops within pentatonic runs. Every technique you've learned applied to the most commonly used scale. This is where it all comes together.

theoryLessons.title: Harmonic Minor Scale
theoryLessons.content: The natural minor scale has a weakness: its V chord is minor, lacking the strong dominant resolution. The harmonic minor raises the 7th degree, creating a major V chord. Formula: 1-2-b3-4-5-b6-7.

keyPoints.definition: W-H-W-W-H-W+H-H (that W+H gap between b6 and 7 is an augmented 2nd — 3 half steps)
A-B-C-D-E-F-G#-A. Only one note different from natural minor: G becomes G#.
F to G# = 3 half steps. This exotic interval gives harmonic minor its distinctive 'Middle Eastern' flavor.
G# creates a leading tone (half step to A). The V chord becomes E major (E-G#-B) instead of Em. Now V→i resolution is strong.

theoryLessons.title: Harmonic Minor Modes Overview
theoryLessons.content: Like the major scale, harmonic minor has 7 modes. The most useful are the 5th mode (Phrygian Dominant — the Spanish/flamenco sound) and the 7th mode (Altered Dominant scale).

keyPoints.definition: Built on the 5th degree. In A harmonic minor: E-F-G#-A-B-C-D. The b2 + major 3rd combination = instant flamenco.
Am → G → F → E7. The E7 uses Phrygian Dominant. Classic Spanish guitar sound.
Built on the 7th degree. Used over altered dominant chords in jazz. Advanced application.

theoryLessons.title: Harmonic Minor on Guitar
theoryLessons.content: The harmonic minor scale is one note different from natural minor — the raised 7th. In your CAGED patterns, find the b7 and raise it one fret. The fingering changes slightly but the shapes are almost identical.

keyPoints.definition: Natural minor: b7 is 2 frets below root. Harmonic minor: 7 is 1 fret below root.
The b6 to 7 gap (augmented 2nd) feels like a stretch on guitar. This is normal — embrace the exotic sound.
Play natural minor for most of a solo, switch to harmonic minor when the V chord hits. The raised 7th resolves beautifully.

routines.name: Triads & 7ths In/Out
routines.connectionDescription: Playing through diatonic 7th chords in and out of position while understanding minor key harmony lets you navigate minor key progressions with complete freedom.

exercises.name: Diatonic 7th Arpeggios — In Position
exercises.description: Play all 7 diatonic 7th arpeggios in C major within one CAGED position. Cmaj7-Dm7-Em7-Fmaj7-G7-Am7-Bm7b5. Stay within a 4-fret span. This tests your knowledge of each chord's shape within the scale position.

exercises.name: Breaking Out of Position
exercises.description: Play a Cmaj7 arpeggio starting in position 1, slide to position 2 mid-arpeggio, continue to position 3. Horizontal movement through arpeggios across the entire neck.

exercises.name: Voice Leading Through Diatonic 7ths
exercises.description: Play through Cmaj7→Dm7→Em7→Fmaj7→G7→Am7→Bm7b5 using the smoothest voice leading possible. Each chord should share as many common tones as possible with the previous chord.

exercises.name: Comping: Triads + 7ths Combined
exercises.description: Comp through a jazz standard progression (Autumn Leaves or similar) using a mix of triad and 7th chord voicings. Switch between 3-note and 4-note voicings for variety.

theoryLessons.title: Harmonic Minor Diatonic Chords
theoryLessons.content: The raised 7th in harmonic minor changes several diatonic chords compared to natural minor. Most importantly, the v chord becomes V (major), and the VII chord becomes vii° (diminished).

keyPoints.definition: i - ii° - III - iv - v - VI - VII
i - ii° - III+ - iv - V - VI - vii°

keyPoints.term: Key change: V instead of v
keyPoints.definition: Em → E major in Am. NOW V→i has dominant resolution.
The raised 7th turns the III chord augmented. C→C+ in Am harmonic minor.

theoryLessons.title: Comparing Three Minor Scales
theoryLessons.content: Natural minor, harmonic minor, and melodic minor each serve different purposes. Natural = default minor sound. Harmonic = strong V chord. Melodic = smooth ascending line. Advanced players switch between all three within a single solo.

keyPoints.definition: 1-2-b3-4-5-b6-b7. Default minor. V chord is minor.
1-2-b3-4-5-b6-7. Raised 7th. V chord is major. Exotic augmented 2nd.
1-2-b3-4-5-6-7. Raised 6th AND 7th. Smooth. Eliminates the augmented 2nd.
Same ascending AND descending (unlike classical which descends as natural minor). Used extensively in jazz.

theoryLessons.title: Minor Key Progression Analysis
theoryLessons.content: Minor key progressions often mix natural and harmonic minor chords. The i and iv come from natural minor, the V7 comes from harmonic minor. This mixing is standard — you're not 'breaking rules,' you're using the right tool for each moment.

keyPoints.definition: Am - Dm - E7 - Am. The Am and Dm are natural minor. E7 comes from harmonic minor.
Am - G - F - E7. Descending bass with a harmonic minor V at the end.
Bm7b5 - E7 - Am. The ii° comes from natural minor, V7 from harmonic minor.

routines.name: Open Voiced Triads
routines.connectionDescription: Chord melody requires harmonizing every melody note with an appropriate chord. Secondary dominants add chromatic passing chords that make arrangements sound professional and sophisticated.

exercises.name: Open (Spread) Triad Voicings
exercises.description: Take a closed triad (R-3-5 on adjacent strings) and spread it across non-adjacent strings. For example, root on string 5, 3rd on string 3, 5th on string 1. Wider voicings sound more open and professional.

exercises.name: Chord Melody — Simple Melodies
exercises.description: Harmonize 'Happy Birthday' or 'Twinkle Twinkle' by placing a chord under each melody note. The melody is always the highest note. Use closed and open triads to harmonize.

exercises.name: Bass + Melody Independence
exercises.description: Play bass notes with your thumb while picking melody notes with fingers. Two independent voices on one guitar. Start with simple: bass on beats 1 and 3, melody on 2 and 4.

exercises.name: Fingerstyle Chord Melody Technique
exercises.description: Full fingerstyle approach: thumb handles bass (strings 4-5-6), index/middle/ring handle melody and inner voices (strings 1-2-3). Play a simple jazz standard arrangement.

theoryLessons.title: What Are Secondary Dominants?
theoryLessons.content: A secondary dominant is a V7 chord borrowed from another key to temporarily target a diatonic chord. V/V means 'the dominant of the dominant.' In C major, V/V = D7 (because D7 is the V of G, and G is the V of C).

keyPoints.definition: D7 → G. D7 is not diatonic to C major, but it's the V of G. It pulls strongly to G.
A7 → Dm. A7 is the V of Dm. Creates a strong pull to the ii chord.
E7 → Am. E7 is the V of Am. Very common in pop and jazz.
C7 → F. Yes, the I chord becomes a dom7! C7 pulls to F like a V pulls to I.

theoryLessons.title: Secondary Dominant Resolution
theoryLessons.content: Every secondary dominant resolves down a 5th (or up a 4th) to its target chord — just like a regular V7→I. The resolution is what makes it 'work.' Without resolution, it sounds random; with resolution, it sounds intentional and sophisticated.

keyPoints.definition: D7 → G (not D7 → Am). The resolution IS the point.
Secondary dominants often create chromatic bass motion: C-C#dim-Dm or C-D7-G.
A secondary dominant briefly makes its target sound like a new 'tonic.' We hear G as 'home' for a moment before returning to C.

theoryLessons.title: Identifying Secondary Dominants
theoryLessons.content: If you see a non-diatonic dominant 7th chord, it's almost certainly a secondary dominant. Identify its target: what chord is a 5th below it? That target should be a diatonic chord in the original key.

keyPoints.definition: E7 → target is Am (a 5th below). Am IS diatonic to C. So E7 = V/vi.
A7 → target is Dm. Dm IS diatonic. A7 = V/ii.
B7 → target is Em. Em IS diatonic. B7 = V/iii.
F#7 → target is B. B is NOT diatonic (it's Bdim). This is probably NOT a secondary dominant — it might be a modulation.

routines.name: Modal Control
routines.connectionDescription: Modal control and borrowed chords are two sides of the same coin. When a song borrows a chord from the parallel minor, the soloist needs to shift modes to match. Instant mode switching aligns with understanding when and why chords are borrowed.

exercises.name: Instant Mode Switching
exercises.description: Play over a static G chord: 4 bars Ionian, 4 bars Lydian, 4 bars Mixolydian. Switch modes without stopping. The chord stays the same — YOUR note choice creates the modal color.

exercises.name: Modal Improvisation Over Vamps
exercises.description: Improvise over single-chord vamps: Dm7 (Dorian), E Phrygian, Bb Lydian, A Mixolydian. Spend 2 minutes on each. Emphasize the characteristic note of each mode.

exercises.name: Targeting Characteristic Notes
exercises.description: In each mode, identify the ONE note that makes it unique. Dorian = natural 6th. Lydian = #4. Phrygian = b2. Mixolydian = b7. Build licks that prominently feature this note.

exercises.name: Mode Mixing in Solos
exercises.description: Over a Dm7-G7 vamp, switch between Dorian (over Dm7) and Mixolydian (over G7) seamlessly. Then try: Dorian over Dm7, altered scale over G7 for a jazz sound.

theoryLessons.title: Parallel Major and Minor Keys
theoryLessons.content: Parallel keys share the same root but use different scales. C major and C minor are parallel keys. They share the root (C) but have different notes. Borrowing chords between parallel keys is one of the most common harmonic techniques.

keyPoints.definition: C-D-E-F-G-A-B (bright, happy)
C-D-Eb-F-G-Ab-Bb (dark, sad)
Three notes differ: E/Eb, A/Ab, B/Bb. These create different chord qualities.
C major and A minor are RELATIVE (same notes, different root). C major and C minor are PARALLEL (same root, different notes).

theoryLessons.title: Borrowing Chords from Parallel Minor
theoryLessons.content: In a major key, you can 'borrow' chords from the parallel minor to add color and drama. The most commonly borrowed chords are bVII, bVI, bIII, and iv.

keyPoints.definition: Bb chord (from C minor). Used in: Hey Jude, Let It Be, every classic rock song.
Ab chord (from C minor). Dramatic, cinematic. Used in James Bond themes, film scores.
Eb chord (from C minor). Creates a powerful tonal shift. Used in Radiohead, Muse.
Fm chord (from C minor). Replaces the IV (F major) for a darker color. 'Creep' by Radiohead.

theoryLessons.title: Modal Interchange in Practice
theoryLessons.content: Modal interchange is the formal term for borrowing between parallel modes. You're not limited to minor → major borrowing. You can borrow from any parallel mode: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian.

keyPoints.definition: bVII chord. C Mixolydian gives you Bb chord in C major.
IV chord becomes minor. Interesting but less common.
II chord becomes major. D major in C major (from C Lydian). Bright, uplifting.
When a borrowed chord appears, briefly switch to the mode it comes from. bVII (Bb) in C major → play C Mixolydian over that bar.

routines.name: Economy/Sweep Picking
routines.connectionDescription: The final routine brings together the most technically demanding picking technique with the most harmonically sophisticated concept. Sweep-picked arpeggios through a modulating progression is the ultimate test — the graduation exercise for the entire curriculum.

exercises.name: Economy Picking Fundamentals
exercises.description: Economy picking uses the direction of the pick to your advantage: when crossing to a higher string, use a downstroke (continuing the motion). When crossing lower, upstroke. No wasted motion.

exercises.name: 3-String Sweep Arpeggio Patterns
exercises.description: Sweep across 3 strings to play triads: Am (fret 5), C (fret 8), etc. The pick 'sweeps' in one continuous motion — down-down-down ascending, up-up-up descending. Each note must ring separately (not strum).

exercises.name: 5-String Sweep Patterns
exercises.description: Expand to 5-string sweep arpeggios. Am7 shape, Cmaj7 shape. The full sweep is down-down-down-down-down ascending, with a hammer-on at the top, then up-up-up-up-up descending with a pull-off.

exercises.name: Musical Application — Sweeps in Context
exercises.description: Don't just run arpeggios up and down — use sweeps as musical phrases within a solo. Sweep into a held note, add vibrato. Sweep through a chord change. Connect sweeps with scale runs. Make it MUSIC, not an exercise.

theoryLessons.title: Direct Modulation
theoryLessons.content: The simplest key change: just move to the new key with no preparation. Abrupt but effective. Common in pop songs that raise the key for the final chorus (the 'truck driver modulation' — usually up a half step or whole step).

keyPoints.definition: Final chorus modulation. Key of C → key of Db. Instant energy lift.
Key of C → key of D. Classic pop/rock move.
Just start playing in the new key. The surprise IS the effect.
My Girl (modulates up a whole step), Love On Top by Beyoncé (modulates 4 times!).

theoryLessons.title: Pivot Chord Modulation
theoryLessons.content: Use a chord that exists in BOTH the old key and the new key as a 'pivot.' The listener doesn't notice the modulation until the new key is established. Smooth and elegant.

keyPoints.definition: List chords in both keys. Find matches. C major and G major share: C, Em, G, Am, Dm (sort of).
Am chord exists in both keys (vi in C, ii in G). Play Am, then follow with D7→G (ii-V-I in G). Smooth transition.
Am (vi in C) can reinterpret as the i chord temporarily, then A7→D leads to D major. But Dm (ii in C) = iv in A isn't standard. Sometimes multiple pivots are needed.

theoryLessons.title: Common-Tone Modulation
theoryLessons.content: Hold a single note (or two) constant while changing the chord beneath it. The sustained note connects the old key to the new key. The smoothest modulation technique.

keyPoints.definition: Hold the note E. Under it, play Cmaj7 (E is the 3rd) → then shift to E major chord (E is the root). E stayed constant but the key changed from C to E.
G# in E major = Ab in Fm. Same pitch, different name. This is how distant modulations work smoothly.
Great for ambient, film score, and jazz. The listener barely notices the key change.
